author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: Overweight, food-obsessed schoolboy Bubber Surle visits an elderly, isolated widow, Mrs. Drew, purely for her fresh-baked cookies, tolerating her requests that he stay and read to her from his schoolbooks as the price of the treat.
page_summary:
Overweight, food-obsessed schoolboy Bubber Surle visits an elderly, isolated widow, Mrs. Drew, purely for her fresh-baked cookies, tolerating her requests that he stay and read to her from his schoolbooks as the price of the treat. Each visit follows the same pattern: as Bubber reads aloud beside her, something happens to Mrs. Drew that neither of them names or fully understands — she grows younger, her wrinkles smoothing, her body filling out with youth, drawing some vital quality directly out of the boy's proximity and voice. The transformation reverses the instant Bubber leaves, and Bubber himself walks home each time strangely exhausted, his heart laboring, though he never connects this to anything Mrs. Drew has done. When Bubber's parents forbid further visits, worried at how drained he looks afterward, he comes one last time to tell her; in her desperation at losing her only source of renewal, Mrs. Drew moves her chair beside him and touches his arm directly, drawing far more from him than before — enough that the transformation does not reverse when he leaves. Restored fully to youthful vitality for the first time, she runs a bath and delights in her new body while Bubber staggers home through a bitter wind, weaker with every step; he collapses before reaching his door, and his parents find only a bundle of dry weeds and rags blown against the porch by the storm, mistaking his remains for windblown trash.

**Why it matters.** Sutin identifies this story directly as one of only two fantasy pieces Dick's editors at Rickett & Cohen (R&C) accepted for a collection, describing it precisely as 'a variation on the Hansel and Gretel theme' — a classification that clarifies the story's genre lineage exactly: an isolated house, a lured child, an adult whose hospitality conceals predation, and a fatal price paid for food freely offered. What makes Dick's version unsettling rather than merely faithful to its source is the total absence of malice or witchcraft as such — Mrs. Drew's hunger reads as pathetic and understandable loneliness escalating past a point of control, not calculated evil, and the story never romanticizes or explains the mechanism of the transfer. The final image, in which Bubber's own father fails to recognize his son's remains, closes the story on a note of horror made worse by its total silence — no one in the story ever learns what actually happened.

*Ralf Surle closes the door on what is left of his son, telling his wife it was 'just the wind' — the story's last line withholding recognition from the one person who might otherwise have understood.*

structure.form: short story in four scenes, structured as a fairy tale of predation disguised as ordinary neighborly kindness
movements: Establishing the visits: cookies as bait, reading as tribute, and the unexplained rejuvenation that occurs only in Bubber's presence.
The parents' growing unease at how drained Bubber looks after each visit, and their decision to forbid further contact.
The final, 'last' visit, in which Mrs. Drew's desperation leads her to touch Bubber directly and draw a fatal, irreversible amount of vitality from him.
Bubber's collapse on the walk home, and his parents mistaking his remains for wind-blown debris.
structure.point_of_view: third person, moving between Bubber's blunt, food-driven interiority and Mrs. Drew's more complex, guilt-tinged hunger, so the reader understands the exchange as predatory well before either character does.
structure.central_device: A vampiric transaction disguised entirely in the vocabulary of ordinary kindness — cookies, companionship, reading aloud — with neither party using or perhaps even possessing the language to name what is actually happening between them.

characters.name: Bubber Surle
characters.note: Entirely motivated by appetite throughout, never suspicious, never analytical — his own greed for cookies is what repeatedly delivers him into the situation that eventually kills him.

characters.name: Mrs. Drew
characters.note: Not portrayed as a witch or a monster by disposition — lonely, apologetic, and genuinely distressed by what she does to herself and, implicitly, to him, right up until desperation at losing him overrides her restraint entirely.

characters.name: May and Ralf Surle
characters.note: Notice the physical toll on their son with real concern and act on it, but too late and for the wrong specific fear — they suspect the old woman is 'strange,' not that she is killing him.

settings.name: Mrs. Drew's house
settings.note: Shabby, overgrown, isolated at the end of the street — the classic fairy-tale witch's cottage rendered in ordinary 1950s suburban terms.

settings.name: The walk home
settings.note: Where the story's horror is finally and literally externalized, as Bubber's collapsing body is carried off and reduced to something his own father cannot recognize as his son.

motifs: Food as both the lure and the cover story for a predatory relationship neither party names
Physical exhaustion in the victim mirroring, in inverse, a rejuvenation in the predator
A transformation that reverses itself except at the fatal moment when restraint finally breaks down
The victim's remains reduced to something unrecognizable and disposable — 'a bundle of gray, dry weeds' mistaken for windblown trash
A fairy-tale structure (an isolated house, a lured child, a hidden appetite) transposed without any fantastical framing device into an ordinary American street

distinctive_terms.label: Book
distinctive_terms.note: Bubber's schoolbooks, the tribute he pays for cookies and the actual mechanism of the transfer, since it is his reading voice that draws Mrs. Drew's youth out of him.

pkd_on_this_work.summary: Dick's letters confirm the story's belated television sale two decades after it was written.

evidence.quote: Here are the signed Metromedia contracts back for the TV rights on "The Cookie Lady" (three copies).
evidence.reading: Dated December 6, 1973 — confirms the specific studio and contract details for the story's television adaptation rights.

evidence.quote: And I made my first (although tiny) U.S. TV sale: an old story, "The Cookie Lady," for $750.
evidence.reading: Dick's own account of the sale's significance — his first American television sale, two decades after the story's original 1953 publication, for a modest sum he nonetheless flags as a milestone.

evidence.author: Lawrence Sutin
evidence.quote: "The Cookie Lady" (w. 1952, p. 1953), a variation on the Hansel and Gretel theme, and the haunting "Upon the Dull Earth" (w. 1953, p. 1954)
evidence.reading: Sutin's direct genre classification — a Hansel and Gretel variant — and pairing with 'Upon the Dull Earth' (also read in this project) as the only two fantasy pieces accepted for a particular collection.

evidence.author: Christopher Palmer
evidence.quote: others include 'The Cookie Lady' (1953, CS2), 'Tony and the Beetles' (1953, CS3), 'Jon's World' (1954, CS2), 'A World of Talent' (1954, CS3),
evidence.reading: Palmer groups this story in a list whose organizing theme was not fully captured in this evidence pass — the surrounding argument should be read to determine what connects it to the other titles named.

open_questions: Palmer's list groups this story with 'Tony and the Beetles', 'Jon's World', and 'A World of Talent' under an argument not fully captured here — worth reading his full passage once those stories are also close-read.
What editorial collection is Sutin referring to when he says only two of Dick's fantasy stories 'made it' past the R&C standard? Identifying it would clarify the story's specific publication history.

The mechanism of the vitality transfer (reading aloud, physical proximity, touch) is never explained by the text. Is there any indication elsewhere of what Dick intended Mrs. Drew actually to be — witch, vampire, or something without a name?

reading_provenance.note: Close reading of the primary text plus attributed evidence from the archive. Candidate: not yet promoted to canonical.

later_use: Sold for U.S. television rights to Metromedia in 1973 for $750 — Dick's first American TV sale.
